title: Kneading bread dough by hand
subtitle: developing gluten in a yeasted dough through repeated stretching and folding
excerpt: Kneading develops the gluten network in bread dough that gives the loaf its structure and chewy texture. The technique involves stretching the dough away from you, folding it back on itself, giving it a quarter turn, and repeating. Most doughs need 8 to 10 minutes of kneading to reach the window-pane stage, where the dough can be stretched thin enough to see light through without tearing.
sourceNotes: Hand-kneading is a fundamental bread-making technique documented in British baking manuals from at least the eighteenth century. Method consistent across Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861, Project Gutenberg #10136) and later British bread-baking resources.

glossaryTerms.definition: A protein network formed when flour and water are mixed and worked together. Gluten gives bread dough its elasticity, allows it to trap carbon dioxide from yeast, and gives the baked loaf its chewy texture and structure.

A check for gluten development: a small piece of dough is stretched slowly between your fingers until it forms a thin, translucent membrane. If the dough tears before becoming translucent, kneading needs to continue.

content.text: strands in the dough. An under-kneaded dough will be sticky and tear easily, giving a dense loaf with a ragged crumb. A properly kneaded dough will feel smooth and elastic, only slightly tacky; it will spring back when poked with a finger.

Work on a clean, unfloured surface. A very lightly oiled surface can help for very sticky doughs, but flour slows gluten development and makes a heavier loaf. Remove any rings or bracelets before starting.
Place the dough on the surface. Push the heel of one hand into the centre of the dough, pushing it away from you. The dough should stretch out.
Fold the far end of the dough back toward you, folding it roughly in half. Give the dough a quarter turn.
Repeat the push, fold, and turn continuously. Build a rhythm. The motion is not aggressive: a firm, steady stretch and fold is more effective than hard pounding.

Tear off a small piece of dough and stretch it gently between your thumbs and index fingers, working outward from the centre. Well-kneaded dough will stretch to a thin, translucent membrane before it tears. If it tears immediately with ragged edges, knead for a further 2 minutes and test again.

attrs.problem: Dough sticking constantly to the surface
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding too much flour to the surface; a little sticking at the start is normal and reduces as gluten develops.
attrs.fix: Use a dough scraper to lift and fold sticky dough from the surface rather than adding flour.

attrs.problem: Dough snapping back immediately and feeling very tight
attrs.avoid: Avoid working with dough that is too cold; cold dough is stiff and slow to develop.
attrs.fix: Rest the dough covered for 5 minutes (autolyse rest) to allow the gluten to relax, then continue kneading.

attrs.problem: Arms tiring before the dough is ready
attrs.avoid: Avoid a short, choppy motion; the push comes from body weight, not arm strength.
attrs.fix: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, lean into the dough from the shoulder, and let your weight do the work.
